notes.5.18: Herikon (line 24) is probably Erichthonius. In line 21 hra is read as hrá, 'raw, untilled'. In line 78 'aſia' is written twice. In line 80 'r' is read as ár, 'good seasons'. Line 86 breaks off at 'ꝼẏ', read as fyrr, 'before'.
notes.4.18: 4.26: 'setja þeir fyrir Óðin', literally 'they set for Odin', i.e. they take Priam to be Odin. 4.31: 'phitonsanda list' renders Latin spiritus pythonis, soothsaying. 5.4: 'uaran' is read as óáran, 'bad year'; uncertain.

nodes.text: Near the middle of the world was built the house and dwelling, the most famous that has
[ever] been built, which was called Troy, in the place we call Turkey. This city was much
larger in build than others, and [made] with more skill in many ways, with the wealth and resources
that were there. There were twelve kingdoms and one high king, and many nations belonged to each
kingdom. There were twelve chief languages in the city. These chieftains have been above
all men who have been in the world in all human things. There is
least doubt about this, whichever learned man has told of them; and because all the leading men of the northern half [of the world]
trace their lineage back there, and place in the number of the gods all who were leaders of the city,
and especially as they set Priam himself in the place of Odin, that cannot be called strange, because
Priam was descended from Saturn, whom the northern half for a long time believed God himself
to have been. This Saturn grew up on the island in the Greek sea that is called Crete. He was bigger and
stronger and handsomer than other men; his wisdom surpassed all men, as did his other natural gifts.
He also discovered many arts that had not been discovered before. He was also so great in that skill
which is called the art of the python-spirit that he knew things before they came to pass. He also found the ore in the earth
from which he smelted gold, and from things of this kind he quickly became powerful. He also foretold the harvests
and many other hidden things, and for this and much else they took him as chieftain over
the island; and when he had ruled it a little while, there was soon abundance there of every kind of good harvest.
No coin passed there but gold coin, so plentiful was it; and though there was famine
in other lands, there was never a bad year there; so [people] could go there for all
the things they needed to have. And because of this and many other unseen gifts of power
that he had, they believed him to be a god; and from this began another error among the men of Crete
and the Macedonians, just as the earlier one [began] among the Assyrians and Chaldeans from Zoroaster. And
when Saturn finds how much strength the people think they have from him, then he declares himself
to be God, and says he is ruler of heaven and earth and of all things.
He had three sons: one was called Jupiter, the second Neptune, the third Pluto. They were all men of accomplishment,
the greatest, and Jupiter was far ahead of them. He was a man of war and won many kings' realms.
He was also cunning, like his father, and took on himself the likenesses of various beasts, and by that means he brought many things
about that are impossible for mankind to do; and because of such things and others
all peoples feared him. Therefore Jupiter is equated with Thor, since all evil beings feared him.
Saturn had seventy-two cities built in Crete, and when he thought himself fully established in
his kingdom, he divided it among his sons, as he set himself up as a god; and he assigned to Jupiter
the kingdom of heaven, and to Neptune the kingdom of earth, and to Pluto hell; and that seemed to him the least desirable portion,
and so he gave him his dog, which he called Cerberus, to guard hell.
This Cerberus the Greeks say Hercules dragged out of hell and up onto the earth. And although
Saturn had allotted heaven to Jupiter, he was no less eager to possess the earth,
and he now makes war on his father's kingdom; and it is said that he had him seized and castrated, and for
such great deeds he declares himself to be a god. And the Macedonians say that he had the genitals taken and thrown
out into the sea, and so they believed for a long time that a woman had come into being from them, whom they called
Venus. And so Venus has ever since been called the goddess of love, and they placed her in the gods'
number, for they believed that she could turn the hearts of all people to love, of men and of women.
When Saturn had been castrated by his son Jupiter, he fled from the east out of Crete and hither
to Italy. At that time peoples of such a kind lived there as did no work and lived on acorns and
plants, and lay in caves or holes in the ground. And when Saturn came there, he changed his name and called
himself Njord, because he thought that his son Jupiter would then be less likely to find him out.
He was the first man there to teach ploughing and the planting of vineyards. The soil there was good and untilled,
and soon there was great plenty there. They took him as their chieftain, and so he gained possession of all such
realms, and had many cities built there. Jupiter his son had many sons, from whom families
have come. His son was Dardanus, his son Herikon, his son Laomedon, the father
of Priam the high king. Priam had many sons. One of them was Hector, who has been the most renowned
of all men in the world for strength and stature and accomplishment and all the manly arts of knightly
breeding. And it is found written that when the Greeks and all the strength of the northern half and the eastern half [of the world]
fought against the men of Troy, they would never have been defeated, had the Greeks not
called on the gods; and the oracles went so, that no human nature could defeat them unless they were
betrayed by their own men, as later happened. And from their fame men who came after took
for themselves their names of honour, especially the Romans, who have been the most renowned of men
in many respects since their day. And it is said that when Rome was completed, the Romans modelled
their customs and law as closely as they could on what the men of Troy,
their forefathers, had had. And such great power went with these men that many
ages later, when Pompey, a chieftain of the Romans, made war in the eastern part [of the world], there fled
away Odin out of Asia and hither into the northern part; and then he gave himself and his men their
names, and said that Priam had been called Odin, and his queen Frigg, and from that the kingdom took
its name afterwards and was called Phrygia, where the city stood. And whether Odin said that out of pride
for himself, or it came about in this way through the change of languages, yet many learned men have
held it to be a true account; and for a long age afterwards, whoever was a great chieftain
took his example from that. One king in Troy was called Munon or Memnon; he married
the daughter of Priam the high king. She was called Troan. They had a son; he was called Tror, the one
we call Thor. He was brought up in Thrace with a duke who is named Loricus. And when
he was ten winters old, he took up his father's weapons. He was so fair to look on when he came
among other men as when ivory is inlaid in oak; his hair is fairer than gold.
When he was twelve winters old he had his full strength; then he lifted from the ground
ten bearskins all at once. And then he killed Duke Loricus, his foster-father, and his wife
Lora or Glora, and took for himself the realm of Thrace, which we call Thrudheim. Then he travelled widely through
lands and explored every quarter of the world, and alone defeated all berserks and all giants, and one
dragon, the greatest, and many beasts. In the northern part of the world he found a prophetess who was called Sibyl,
whom we call Sif, and married her. No one can tell Sif's lineage. She was the fairest of all women;
her hair was like gold. Their son was Loridi, who was like his father. His son was Henredi;
his [son] Vingethor; his son Vingener; his son Moda; his son Magi; his son Cespheth;
his son Bedvig; his son Athra, whom we call Annan; his son Itrmann; his son Heremod;
his son Skaldun, whom we call Skjold; his son Biaf, whom we call Biar; his son
Iat; his son Gudolf; his son Finn; his son Friallaf, whom we call Fridleif. He had the
son who is named Voden; him we call Odin. He was a renowned man for wisdom and every
accomplishment. His wife was called Frigida, whom we call Frigg. Odin had the gift of prophecy, and so had his wife,
and through that knowledge he found that his name would be kept alive in the northern part
of the world and honoured above all kings. For that reason he was eager to begin his journey from
Turkland, and had with him a great multitude of people, young men and old, men and women; and
they had with them many precious things. And wherever they went through lands, great renown
was spoken of them, so that they seemed more like gods than men. And they make no halt on their journey
until they come north into the land which is now called Saxland. There Odin stayed a long
while and took possession of that land far and wide. There Odin set to guard the land
three of his sons. One is named Veggde; he was a powerful king and ruled over East Saxland. His son
was Vitrgils. His sons were Picta, the father of Hengist, and Siga, the father of Svebdeg, whom we call
Svipdag. The second son of Odin was called Beldeg, whom we call Baldr. He held the land which is now called
Westphalia. His son was Brand; his son Friodigar, whom we call Frodi; his son was Freovin;
his son Yvi; his son Gevis, whom we call Gave. And the third son of Odin is named Sigi;
his son Rerir. These forefathers ruled over what is now called Frankland, and from them comes that family
which is called the Volsungs. From all of these great families have come, and many.
Then Odin began his journey north and came into the land which they called
Reidgotaland, and took possession in that land of all that he wished. He set his son there over the land,
who was called Skjold. His son was Fridleif. From him comes the family called the Skjoldungs;
they are the kings of the Danes. And what was then called Reidgotaland is now called Jutland.
After that he went north to where it is now called Sweden. There was a king there who is named Gylfi.
And when he learned of the coming of those men of Asia, who were called Aesir, he went to meet them and
offered that Odin should have as much power in his kingdom as he himself wished. And such good fortune went with
their journey that wherever they stayed in any land there were good seasons and peace. They all believed that they
were the cause of it, because men of rank saw that they were unlike other men whom they had seen,
in beauty and in wisdom too. Odin found the land fair and fruitful there, and he chose a site for a city there, at what is now
called Sigtuna; that was [named] from his name. And he took royal rule and called himself Njord; and so it is found written
in books of learning that the first king of the Swedes was called Njord. The reason for that is that Odin was
the most noble there. And he appointed chieftains there after the likeness of what there had been in Troy:
he set twelve chief men in the city to judge the laws of the land, and he ordered all rights just as before
they had been in Troy, and as the Turks were used to. After that he went north until
the sea stopped him, the sea they thought lay around all lands; and he set his son over the realm
which is now called Norway. He was called Saeming, and the kings of Norway trace their lineage to him, and so do
jarls and other men of rank, as it says in Haleygjatal. And Odin had with him that
son of his who is named Yngvi, who was king in Sweden after him; and from him come those
families which are called the Ynglings. The Aesir took themselves wives there within the land, and some for their sons,
